tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

1	# linkvault: Interface Contract
2	
3	## Constraints
4	
5	- **Stack:** Python >=3.11, stdlib only (`http.server`, `sqlite3`, `json`, `argparse`, `urllib`, `secrets`, `hashlib`, `threading`, `signal`); pytest for tests only.
6	- **Package location:** `linkvault/` at the workspace root (`linkvault/__init__.py`, `linkvault/__main__.py`); commands run with the workspace root as cwd.
7	- **Entry points:** `python -m linkvault serve ...` (server); `python -m linkvault <client-cmd> ...` (client).
8	
9	## Functional requirements
10	
11	- **R1 Server start.** `serve` opens or creates the DB, binds 127.0.0.1, then prints exactly one ready line to stdout. Nothing else is ever written to stdout; logs go to stderr.
12	- **R2 Token issuance.** `POST /v1/tokens` with the correct admin key returns a new token. The token is `lv_` followed by 32 lowercase hex characters (`secrets.token_hex(16)`). Only its SHA-256 hex digest is stored.
13	- **R3 Authentication.** Every `/v1/links` route requires `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. A missing, malformed or unknown token returns 401.
14	- **R4 Create link.** `POST /v1/links` stores `url` with a custom `slug` or a generated slug, and an optional `expires_in`.
15	- **R5 Slug rules.** Slugs are case-sensitive. A custom slug must match `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{3,32}$` and must not be `healthz`. A generated slug is 7 characters from `abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789`, drawn with `secrets.choice`. It is regenerated if it already exists or is reserved, with up to 5 attempts and then 500. Creating an existing slug returns 409.
16	- **R6 URL rules.** The scheme is `http` or `https` (case-insensitive). `urllib.parse.urlsplit(url).hostname` is non-empty. The URL is at most 2048 characters and contains no whitespace or control characters (code points < 0x21 or 0x7F). It is stored and redirected to verbatim.
17	- **R7 Resolve.** `GET /<slug>` returns 302 with `Location: <url>` and an empty body. It atomically increments `clicks` and sets `last_clicked_at` to now.
18	- **R8 Missing and expired links.** An unknown slug returns 404. A link with `now >= expires_at` returns 410 and its click count is unchanged. Comparisons use whole seconds.
19	- **R9 List and inspect.** A token can list its own links (expired ones included) and fetch one link with its stats. Another token's link always returns 404, never 403.
20	- **R10 Delete.** A token can delete its own link. Afterwards the slug resolves 404 and is free to reuse.
21	- **R11 Rate limit.** Requests are counted per token in fixed 60-second windows aligned to the Unix epoch (`window_start = now - now % 60`). The limit is `--rate-limit` (default 60) counted requests per window. A request is counted when it reaches the rate-limit step (see precedence in Error handling), whatever its final status. Request number `limit + 1` and later in the same window return 429 with `Retry-After: <window_start + 60 - now>`. Counters are in memory and reset on restart. Redirects, `/healthz` and admin routes are not rate-limited.
22	- **R12 Clock.** "Now" is integer Unix seconds (floor of real time). With `--fake-clock <ISO>`, now is frozen at that instant and changes only through `POST /v1/admin/clock`. The fake clock is not persisted.
23	- **R13 Persistence.** Tokens, links, clicks and `last_clicked_at` survive a restart on the same `--db`.
24	- **R14 Concurrency.** The server is a `ThreadingHTTPServer`. N concurrent redirects to one slug leave `clicks == N` exactly.
25	- **R15 Shutdown.** On SIGINT, SIGTERM (POSIX) or CTRL_BREAK_EVENT/SIGBREAK (Windows), the server stops accepting connections, closes the DB and exits 0 within 5 seconds.
26	- **R16 Client.** CLI commands wrap the API. Each prints the response body to stdout, and uses the exit codes below.
27	
28	## Interface contract
29	
30	### Conventions
31	
32	- Timestamps are `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ` in UTC with whole seconds. They are stored as INTEGER Unix seconds.
33	- JSON responses are encoded with `json.dumps(obj, separators=(",", ":"), ensure_ascii=True)` in UTF-8, with `Content-Type: application/json`. Every response sets `Content-Length`; a 204 response has an empty body and MUST send `Content-Length: 0`. Keys appear in exactly the order listed below.
34	- Request `Content-Type` is ignored. The body is read using `Content-Length` (absent means empty), and the maximum is 8192 bytes.
35	- Query strings are ignored on every route. Paths are matched exactly, with no trailing-slash normalisation. Any (method, path) pair not listed below returns 404 `not_found`.
36	- `short_url` is `http://127.0.0.1:<bound port>/<slug>`.
37	
38	**Link object** (key order is fixed): `{"slug", "url", "short_url", "created_at", "expires_at", "clicks", "last_clicked_at"}`. `expires_at` and `last_clicked_at` are `null` until they are set.
39	
40	### Server CLI
41	
42	```
43	python -m linkvault serve --db PATH --admin-key KEY [--port N] [--rate-limit N] [--fake-clock ISO]
44	```
45	
46	| Flag | Rule |
47	|---|---|
48	| `--db` | Required. The file is created if missing, and its parent directory must exist. |
49	| `--admin-key` | Required. Non-empty string. |
50	| `--port` | 0-65535, default 8000. The value 0 binds an OS-chosen free port. |
51	| `--rate-limit` | Integer >= 1, default 60. |
52	| `--fake-clock` | An ISO timestamp in the format above. It enables the admin clock route. |
53	
54	Ready line: `LISTENING http://127.0.0.1:<port>` followed by a line terminator, which may be `\n` or `\r\n`. It uses the actual bound port, is flushed immediately, and nothing else is written to stdout before it.
55	
56	Exit codes: 0 for a clean shutdown; 2 for a usage error (argparse); 3 if the port cannot be bound or the DB cannot be opened, with a message to stderr.
57	
58	### Endpoints
59	
60	| # | Method and path | Auth | Request body | Success response |
61	|---|---|---|---|---|
62	| E1 | `GET /healthz` | none | none | 200 `{"status":"ok"}` |
63	| E2 | `POST /v1/tokens` | `X-Admin-Key: <key>` | ignored | 201 `{"token":"lv_…","created_at":"…"}` |
64	| E3 | `POST /v1/links` | Bearer | `{"url": str, "slug"?: str, "expires_in"?: int}` | 201, link object |
65	| E4 | `GET /v1/links` | Bearer | none | 200 `{"links":[link…]}` ordered by `created_at` ascending, then `slug` ascending |
66	| E5 | `GET /v1/links/<slug>` | Bearer | none | 200, link object |
67	| E6 | `DELETE /v1/links/<slug>` | Bearer | none | 204, empty body |
68	| E7 | `GET /<slug>` | none | none | 302, `Location: <url>`, `Content-Length: 0`, empty body |
69	| E8 | `POST /v1/admin/clock` | `X-Admin-Key` | `{"now": ISO}` | 200 `{"now":"…"}`. The route exists only with `--fake-clock`; otherwise it returns 404. Any valid timestamp is accepted. |
70	
71	E3 body rules:
72	- The body is a JSON object with no extra keys.
73	- `url` is required and must follow R6.
74	- `slug` is optional and must follow R5. An explicit `null` is `invalid_request` (400).
75	- `expires_in` is optional. It is an integer from 1 to 31536000, and `bool` values are rejected. An explicit `null` is `invalid_request` (400). It sets `expires_at = created_at + expires_in`.

77	E8 body rules:
78	- The body must be exactly `{"now": ISO}`, where ISO is a string in the timestamp format above.
79	- A missing `now` key, an extra key, a wrong type or an unparseable timestamp returns 400 `invalid_request`.
80	
81	A wrong or missing admin key on E2 or E8 returns 401. On E5, E6 and E7, a `<slug>` that fails `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{3,32}$` is a route mismatch, so it returns 404 at the route step, before auth.

83	### DB schema (exact)
84	
85	```sql
86	PRAGMA user_version = 1;
87	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS tokens (
88	  token_hash TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
89	  created_at INTEGER NOT NULL);
90	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS links (
91	  slug TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
92	  url TEXT NOT NULL,
93	  token_hash TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES tokens(token_hash),
94	  created_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
95	  expires_at INTEGER,
96	  clicks INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
97	  last_clicked_at INTEGER);
98	```
99	
100	A click is recorded with one statement: `UPDATE links SET clicks = clicks + 1, last_clicked_at = ? WHERE slug = ?`.
101	
102	### Client CLI
103	
104	The server URL comes from `--server URL`, or else the `LINKVAULT_SERVER` environment variable. The token comes from `--token T`, or else `LINKVAULT_TOKEN`. Both options are accepted after the subcommand.
105	
106	| Command | Calls | Stdout on success |
107	|---|---|---|
108	| `token create --admin-key K` | E2 | Response JSON, one line |
109	| `shorten URL [--slug S] [--expires-in N]` | E3 | Response JSON, one line |
110	| `list` | E4 | Response JSON, one line |
111	| `stats SLUG` | E5 | Response JSON, one line |
112	| `delete SLUG` | E6 | Nothing |
113	
114	Output is re-serialised with the server's `json.dumps` settings and ends with `\n`. Client exit codes:
115	
116	| Code | Meaning | Output |
117	|---|---|---|
118	| 0 | 2xx response | as above |
119	| 1 | non-2xx response | Error JSON on stderr, stdout empty |
120	| 2 | usage error, or a missing server or token | Message on stderr |
121	| 3 | connection failure | Message on stderr |
122	
123	## Error handling
124	
125	Every error body has this shape: `{"error":{"code":"<code>","message":"<text>"}}`. Tests assert `code` only.
126	
127	| Condition | Status | code |
128	|---|---|---|
129	| No route matches the method and path; unknown or foreign slug | 404 | `not_found` |
130	| Missing, malformed or unknown bearer token; bad admin key | 401 | `unauthorized` |
131	| Over the rate limit (adds a `Retry-After` header) | 429 | `rate_limited` |
132	| `Content-Length` > 8192 (the response sets `Connection: close` and the body is not read) | 413 | `payload_too_large` |
133	| Body is not valid UTF-8 JSON, or is not an object | 400 | `invalid_json` |
134	| Schema violation: missing or extra key, wrong type, bad URL, slug, `expires_in` or `now` | 400 | `invalid_request` |
135	| Slug already exists, or is reserved (`healthz`) | 409 | `slug_taken` |
136	| Link expired (E7 only) | 410 | `gone` |
137	| Unhandled exception | 500 | `internal` |
138	
139	Precedence (first failure wins): route 404 → auth 401 → rate limit 429 → size 413 → JSON 400 → validation 400 → resource state 404/409/410.
140	
141	## Acceptance criteria
142	
143	- **AC1 (R1, R15):** `serve --port 0` prints exactly the `LISTENING` line. `GET /healthz` returns 200. SIGINT (or CTRL_BREAK_EVENT on Windows) makes it exit 0 within 5 s.
144	- **AC2 (R2):** E2 with the right key returns 201 and a token matching `^lv_[0-9a-f]{32}$`. With a wrong key it returns 401. The DB holds the SHA-256 of the token, never the plaintext.

146	- **AC4 (R4, R5):** E3 without `slug` returns a slug matching `^[a-z0-9]{7}$`. A custom `slug` is echoed back. A repeated slug returns 409. `healthz` and `ab` return 409 and 400 respectively.
147	- **AC5 (R6):** `ftp://x`, `javascript:alert(1)`, `http://`, a URL with a space, and a 2049-character URL each return 400 `invalid_request`.
148	- **AC6 (R7):** `GET /<slug>` returns 302 with the exact `Location`. A later E5 shows `clicks` 1 and `last_clicked_at` set to now.
149	- **AC7 (R8, R12):** With the fake clock at T and `expires_in=60`, the link resolves 302 at T+59 and 410 at T+60. Its clicks stay at the T+59 value.

151	- **AC9 (R11):** With `--rate-limit 3` and the fake clock at a window start plus 10 s, requests 1-3 succeed. Request 4 returns 429 with `Retry-After: 50`. After the clock moves to the next window, the next request succeeds. Redirects are never limited.
152	- **AC10 (R13):** After a restart on the same DB, tokens still authenticate, and links and clicks are unchanged.
153	- **AC11 (R14):** 50 concurrent `GET /<slug>` requests leave `clicks == 50`.
154	- **AC12 (R16):** `shorten` prints the link JSON and exits 0. A 409 makes it exit 1 with empty stdout. An unreachable server makes it exit 3. A missing token makes it exit 2.

Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

1	# linkvault: Interface Contract
2	
3	## Constraints
4	
5	- **Stack:** Python >=3.11, stdlib only (`http.server`, `sqlite3`, `json`, `argparse`, `urllib`, `secrets`, `hashlib`, `threading`, `signal`); pytest for tests only.
6	- **Package location:** `linkvault/` at the workspace root (`linkvault/__init__.py`, `linkvault/__main__.py`); commands run with the workspace root as cwd.
7	- **Entry points:** `python -m linkvault serve ...` (server); `python -m linkvault <client-cmd> ...` (client).
8	
9	## Functional requirements
10	
11	- **R1 Server start.** `serve` opens or creates the DB, binds 127.0.0.1, then prints exactly one ready line to stdout. Nothing else is ever written to stdout; logs go to stderr.
12	- **R2 Token issuance.** `POST /v1/tokens` with the correct admin key returns a new token. The token is `lv_` followed by 32 lowercase hex characters (`secrets.token_hex(16)`). Only its SHA-256 hex digest is stored.
13	- **R3 Authentication.** Every `/v1/links` route requires `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. A missing, malformed or unknown token returns 401.
14	- **R4 Create link.** `POST /v1/links` stores `url` with a custom `slug` or a generated slug, and an optional `expires_in`.
15	- **R5 Slug rules.** Slugs are case-sensitive. A custom slug must match `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{3,32}$` and must not be `healthz`. A generated slug is 7 characters from `abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789`, drawn with `secrets.choice`. It is regenerated if it already exists or is reserved, with up to 5 attempts and then 500. Creating an existing slug returns 409.
16	- **R6 URL rules.** The scheme is `http` or `https` (case-insensitive). `urllib.parse.urlsplit(url).hostname` is non-empty. The URL is at most 2048 characters and contains no whitespace or control characters (code points < 0x21 or 0x7F). It is stored and redirected to verbatim.
17	- **R7 Resolve.** `GET /<slug>` returns 302 with `Location: <url>` and an empty body. It atomically increments `clicks` and sets `last_clicked_at` to now.
18	- **R8 Missing and expired links.** An unknown slug returns 404. A link with `now >= expires_at` returns 410 and its click count is unchanged. Comparisons use whole seconds.
19	- **R9 List and inspect.** A token can list its own links (expired ones included) and fetch one link with its stats. Another token's link always returns 404, never 403.
20	- **R10 Delete.** A token can delete its own link. Afterwards the slug resolves 404 and is free to reuse.
21	- **R11 Rate limit.** Requests are counted per token in fixed 60-second windows aligned to the Unix epoch (`window_start = now - now % 60`). The limit is `--rate-limit` (default 60) counted requests per window. A request is counted when it reaches the rate-limit step (see precedence in Error handling), whatever its final status. Request number `limit + 1` and later in the same window return 429 with `Retry-After: <window_start + 60 - now>`. Counters are in memory and reset on restart. Redirects, `/healthz` and admin routes are not rate-limited.
22	- **R12 Clock.** "Now" is integer Unix seconds (floor of real time). With `--fake-clock <ISO>`, now is frozen at that instant and changes only through `POST /v1/admin/clock`. The fake clock is not persisted.
23	- **R13 Persistence.** Tokens, links, clicks and `last_clicked_at` survive a restart on the same `--db`.
24	- **R14 Concurrency.** The server is a `ThreadingHTTPServer`. N concurrent redirects to one slug leave `clicks == N` exactly.
25	- **R15 Shutdown.** On SIGINT, SIGTERM (POSIX) or CTRL_BREAK_EVENT/SIGBREAK (Windows), the server stops accepting connections, closes the DB and exits 0 within 5 seconds.
26	- **R16 Client.** CLI commands wrap the API. Each prints the response body to stdout, and uses the exit codes below.
27	
28	## Interface contract
29	
30	### Conventions
31	
32	- Timestamps are `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ` in UTC with whole seconds. They are stored as INTEGER Unix seconds.
33	- JSON responses are encoded with `json.dumps(obj, separators=(",", ":"), ensure_ascii=True)` in UTF-8, with `Content-Type: application/json`. Every response sets `Content-Length`; a 204 response has an empty body and MUST send `Content-Length: 0`. Keys appear in exactly the order listed below.
34	- Request `Content-Type` is ignored. The body is read using `Content-Length` (absent means empty), and the maximum is 8192 bytes.
35	- Query strings are ignored on every route. Paths are matched exactly, with no trailing-slash normalisation. Any (method, path) pair not listed below returns 404 `not_found`.
36	- `short_url` is `http://127.0.0.1:<bound port>/<slug>`.
37	
38	**Link object** (key order is fixed): `{"slug", "url", "short_url", "created_at", "expires_at", "clicks", "last_clicked_at"}`. `expires_at` and `last_clicked_at` are `null` until they are set.
39	
40	### Server CLI
41	
42	```
43	python -m linkvault serve --db PATH --admin-key KEY [--port N] [--rate-limit N] [--fake-clock ISO]
44	```
45	
46	| Flag | Rule |
47	|---|---|
48	| `--db` | Required. The file is created if missing, and its parent directory must exist. |
49	| `--admin-key` | Required. Non-empty string. |
50	| `--port` | 0-65535, default 8000. The value 0 binds an OS-chosen free port. |
51	| `--rate-limit` | Integer >= 1, default 60. |
52	| `--fake-clock` | An ISO timestamp in the format above. It enables the admin clock route. |
53	
54	Ready line: `LISTENING http://127.0.0.1:<port>` followed by a line terminator, which may be `\n` or `\r\n`. It uses the actual bound port, is flushed immediately, and nothing else is written to stdout before it.
55	
56	Exit codes: 0 for a clean shutdown; 2 for a usage error (argparse); 3 if the port cannot be bound or the DB cannot be opened, with a message to stderr.
57	
58	### Endpoints
59	
60	| # | Method and path | Auth | Request body | Success response |
61	|---|---|---|---|---|
62	| E1 | `GET /healthz` | none | none | 200 `{"status":"ok"}` |
63	| E2 | `POST /v1/tokens` | `X-Admin-Key: <key>` | ignored | 201 `{"token":"lv_…","created_at":"…"}` |
64	| E3 | `POST /v1/links` | Bearer | `{"url": str, "slug"?: str, "expires_in"?: int}` | 201, link object |
65	| E4 | `GET /v1/links` | Bearer | none | 200 `{"links":[link…]}` ordered by `created_at` ascending, then `slug` ascending |
66	| E5 | `GET /v1/links/<slug>` | Bearer | none | 200, link object |
67	| E6 | `DELETE /v1/links/<slug>` | Bearer | none | 204, empty body |
68	| E7 | `GET /<slug>` | none | none | 302, `Location: <url>`, `Content-Length: 0`, empty body |
69	| E8 | `POST /v1/admin/clock` | `X-Admin-Key` | `{"now": ISO}` | 200 `{"now":"…"}`. The route exists only with `--fake-clock`; otherwise it returns 404. Any valid timestamp is accepted. |
70	
71	E3 body rules:
72	- The body is a JSON object with no extra keys.
73	- `url` is required and must follow R6.
74	- `slug` is optional and must follow R5. An explicit `null` is `invalid_request` (400).
75	- `expires_in` is optional. It is an integer from 1 to 31536000, and `bool` values are rejected. An explicit `null` is `invalid_request` (400). It sets `expires_at = created_at + expires_in`.
76	
77	E8 body rules:
78	- The body must be exactly `{"now": ISO}`, where ISO is a string in the timestamp format above.
79	- A missing `now` key, an extra key, a wrong type or an unparseable timestamp returns 400 `invalid_request`.
80	
81	A wrong or missing admin key on E2 or E8 returns 401. On E5, E6 and E7, a `<slug>` that fails `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{3,32}$` is a route mismatch, so it returns 404 at the route step, before auth.
82	
83	### DB schema (exact)
84	
85	```sql
86	PRAGMA user_version = 1;
87	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS tokens (
88	  token_hash TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
89	  created_at INTEGER NOT NULL);
90	CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS links (
91	  slug TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
92	  url TEXT NOT NULL,
93	  token_hash TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES tokens(token_hash),
94	  created_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
95	  expires_at INTEGER,
96	  clicks INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
97	  last_clicked_at INTEGER);
98	```
99	
100	A click is recorded with one statement: `UPDATE links SET clicks = clicks + 1, last_clicked_at = ? WHERE slug = ?`.
101	
102	### Client CLI
103	
104	The server URL comes from `--server URL`, or else the `LINKVAULT_SERVER` environment variable. The token comes from `--token T`, or else `LINKVAULT_TOKEN`. Both options are accepted after the subcommand.
105	
106	| Command | Calls | Stdout on success |
107	|---|---|---|
108	| `token create --admin-key K` | E2 | Response JSON, one line |
109	| `shorten URL [--slug S] [--expires-in N]` | E3 | Response JSON, one line |
110	| `list` | E4 | Response JSON, one line |
111	| `stats SLUG` | E5 | Response JSON, one line |
112	| `delete SLUG` | E6 | Nothing |
113	
114	Output is re-serialised with the server's `json.dumps` settings and ends with `\n`. Client exit codes:
115	
116	| Code | Meaning | Output |
117	|---|---|---|
118	| 0 | 2xx response | as above |
119	| 1 | non-2xx response | Error JSON on stderr, stdout empty |
120	| 2 | usage error, or a missing server or token | Message on stderr |
121	| 3 | connection failure | Message on stderr |
122	
123	## Error handling
124	
125	Every error body has this shape: `{"error":{"code":"<code>","message":"<text>"}}`. Tests assert `code` only.
126	
127	| Condition | Status | code |
128	|---|---|---|
129	| No route matches the method and path; unknown or foreign slug | 404 | `not_found` |
130	| Missing, malformed or unknown bearer token; bad admin key | 401 | `unauthorized` |
131	| Over the rate limit (adds a `Retry-After` header) | 429 | `rate_limited` |
132	| `Content-Length` > 8192 (the response sets `Connection: close` and the body is not read) | 413 | `payload_too_large` |
133	| Body is not valid UTF-8 JSON, or is not an object | 400 | `invalid_json` |
134	| Schema violation: missing or extra key, wrong type, bad URL, slug, `expires_in` or `now` | 400 | `invalid_request` |
135	| Slug already exists, or is reserved (`healthz`) | 409 | `slug_taken` |
136	| Link expired (E7 only) | 410 | `gone` |
137	| Unhandled exception | 500 | `internal` |
138	
139	Precedence (first failure wins): route 404 → auth 401 → rate limit 429 → size 413 → JSON 400 → validation 400 → resource state 404/409/410.
140	
141	## Acceptance criteria
142	
143	- **AC1 (R1, R15):** `serve --port 0` prints exactly the `LISTENING` line. `GET /healthz` returns 200. SIGINT (or CTRL_BREAK_EVENT on Windows) makes it exit 0 within 5 s.
144	- **AC2 (R2):** E2 with the right key returns 201 and a token matching `^lv_[0-9a-f]{32}$`. With a wrong key it returns 401. The DB holds the SHA-256 of the token, never the plaintext.
145	- **AC3 (R3):** E3, E4 and E5 without a valid bearer token return 401 `unauthorized`.
146	- **AC4 (R4, R5):** E3 without `slug` returns a slug matching `^[a-z0-9]{7}$`. A custom `slug` is echoed back. A repeated slug returns 409. `healthz` and `ab` return 409 and 400 respectively.
147	- **AC5 (R6):** `ftp://x`, `javascript:alert(1)`, `http://`, a URL with a space, and a 2049-character URL each return 400 `invalid_request`.
148	- **AC6 (R7):** `GET /<slug>` returns 302 with the exact `Location`. A later E5 shows `clicks` 1 and `last_clicked_at` set to now.
149	- **AC7 (R8, R12):** With the fake clock at T and `expires_in=60`, the link resolves 302 at T+59 and 410 at T+60. Its clicks stay at the T+59 value.
150	- **AC8 (R9, R10):** Token B gets 404 on E5 and E6 for token A's slug. A's E4 lists only A's links in order. After E6, `GET /<slug>` returns 404 and the slug can be created again.
151	- **AC9 (R11):** With `--rate-limit 3` and the fake clock at a window start plus 10 s, requests 1-3 succeed. Request 4 returns 429 with `Retry-After: 50`. After the clock moves to the next window, the next request succeeds. Redirects are never limited.
152	- **AC10 (R13):** After a restart on the same DB, tokens still authenticate, and links and clicks are unchanged.
153	- **AC11 (R14):** 50 concurrent `GET /<slug>` requests leave `clicks == 50`.
154	- **AC12 (R16):** `shorten` prints the link JSON and exits 0. A 409 makes it exit 1 with empty stdout. An unreachable server makes it exit 3. A missing token makes it exit 2.

# `socketserver` – exact statements

## `BaseServer.shutdown()`
> "Tell the `serve_forever()` loop to stop and wait until it does. `shutdown()` must be called while `serve_forever()` is running in a different thread otherwise it will deadlock."

So calling it from the thread running `serve_forever()` (e.g., from inside a handler on a non-threading server) deadlocks. The docs example runs `serve_forever` in a separate thread and calls `server.shutdown()` from the main thread:

```python
server_thread = threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever)
server_thread.daemon = True
server_thread.start()
...
server.shutdown()
```

## `BaseServer.server_close()`
> "Clean up the server. May be overridden."

- Calling it is the last step of creating a server: "Finally, call `server_close()` to close the socket (unless you used a `with` statement)."
- Context-manager support (added 3.6): "Exiting the context manager is equivalent to calling `server_close()`."
- The mixins change its behaviour (see below):
  - `ForkingMixIn.server_close` waits for all child processes.
  - `ThreadingMixIn.server_close` waits for all non-daemon threads.

## `ThreadingMixIn.daemon_threads`
> "For `ThreadingMixIn` use daemonic threads by setting `ThreadingMixIn.daemon_threads` to `True` to not wait until threads complete."

Related guidance: you "should explicitly declare how you want your threads to behave on an abrupt shutdown." The default is `False`, "meaning that Python will not exit until all threads created by `ThreadingMixIn` have exited."

## `block_on_close`
> "`ForkingMixIn.server_close` waits until all child processes complete, except if `block_on_close` attribute is `False`."
>
> "`ThreadingMixIn.server_close` waits until all non-daemon threads complete, except if `block_on_close` attribute is `False`."

Changed in 3.7: `server_close` began waiting for child processes and non-daemonic threads. `block_on_close` was added as an opt-in to the pre-3.7 behaviour.

## `server_address`
> "The address on which the server is listening. The format of addresses varies depending on the protocol family; see the documentation for the `socket` module for details. For internet protocols, this is a tuple containing a string giving the address, and an integer port number: `('127.0.0.1', 80)`, for example."

It is also the first constructor parameter, stored in this attribute. This is useful when binding to port 0 (an arbitrary unused port), as in the docs example:

```python
server = ThreadedTCPServer(("localhost", 0), ThreadedTCPRequestHandler)
with server:
    ip, port = server.server_address
```

## Practical combination
Setting `daemon_threads = True` makes threads daemonic, so they aren't waited on. Setting `block_on_close = False` stops `server_close()` from waiting, restoring the pre-3.7 behaviour. Leaving the defaults means `server_close()` (and the `with` exit) blocks until non-daemon handler threads finish.

# Windows caveats for `signal` (Python 3.15 docs)

## Signals accepted by `signal.signal()` on Windows

> "On Windows, `signal()` can only be called with `SIGABRT`, `SIGFPE`, `SIGILL`, `SIGINT`, `SIGSEGV`, `SIGTERM`, or `SIGBREAK`. A `ValueError` will be raised in any other case."

Also, if a signal name isn't defined on the platform, you get an `AttributeError`, because "only those names defined by the system are defined by this module."

```python
import signal
signal.signal(signal.SIGBREAK, lambda s, f: print("break"))  # OK on Windows
signal.signal(signal.SIGUSR1, ...)  # AttributeError: not defined on Windows
```

## SIGBREAK

> "Interrupt from keyboard (CTRL + BREAK)." Availability: Windows.

## CTRL_C_EVENT / CTRL_BREAK_EVENT

> "The signal corresponding to the Ctrl+Break keystroke event. This signal can only be used with `os.kill()`."

The same restriction applies to `CTRL_C_EVENT`. Both are Windows-only and were added in 3.2. They are not handler targets for `signal.signal()`. You send them with `os.kill(pid, signal.CTRL_BREAK_EVENT)`, and the receiving process observes them as `SIGINT` / `SIGBREAK`.

## SIGTERM

The page makes no Windows-specific claims about `SIGTERM` behavior beyond listing it among the signals `signal.signal()` accepts. The docs only say "Termination signal." If you need to know what actually triggers it on Windows, this page doesn't say.

## Handlers run only in the main thread

> "Python signal handlers are always executed in the main Python thread of the main interpreter, even if the signal was received in another thread."

> "only the main thread of the main interpreter is allowed to set a new signal handler."

Calling `signal.signal()` from another thread raises `ValueError`. Because of this, signals can't be used for inter-thread communication, so use `threading` primitives instead.

## Handlers run between bytecodes

> "the low-level signal handler sets a flag which tells the virtual machine to execute the corresponding Python signal handler at a later point (for example, at the next bytecode instruction)."

Consequences:
- Long-running C calculations (e.g. big regex matches) delay handlers until they finish.
- Exceptions raised in a handler appear "out of thin air" in the main thread, possibly after any bytecode. `KeyboardInterrupt` can therefore strike at awkward points. Robust apps should install their own `SIGINT` handler instead of relying on catching it.
- Don't use locks like `threading.Lock` inside handlers, since this can deadlock.

## Other notes

- `signal.set_wakeup_fd()` on Windows "now also supports socket handles" (changed in 3.5).
- Many functions (`alarm`, `pause`, `pthread_kill`, `setitimer`, `sigwait`, etc.) are Unix-only and unavailable on Windows.

Here is what the page says about each item. Some of your items aren't fully covered by this page, and I've marked those.

**protocol_version default**
> "For backwards compatibility, the setting defaults to `'HTTP/1.0'`."

If set to `'HTTP/1.1'`, persistent connections are permitted, but the server "*must* then include an accurate `Content-Length` header" in all responses. The CLI equivalent is `python -m http.server --protocol HTTP/1.1`.

**log_message behavior (stderr)**
> "Logs an arbitrary message to `sys.stderr`. This is typically overridden to create custom error logging mechanisms."

- `format` is a printf-style string, and the extra arguments are applied to it.
- The client IP address and current date and time are prefixed to every message.
- Since 3.12, control characters are scrubbed in stderr logs. Earlier versions let remote clients send "nefarious control codes" to your terminal.
- `log_error()` passes its message to `log_message()` by default.

**send_error behavior and Connection close**
> "Sends and logs a complete error reply to the client."

- It takes `code`, an optional short `message`, and an optional `explain`, which is formatted with `error_message_format` and sent as the body after the headers.
- Defaults come from `responses`. Unknown codes get `???`.
- The body is empty for HEAD requests and for 1xx, 204, 205 and 304 responses.
- Since 3.4 the response includes a `Content-Length` header.
- **Not covered:** this page says nothing about `send_error` sending a `Connection: close` header. That behavior is in the source (`Lib/http/server.py`), not in this documentation. The only related documented item is `close_connection` (below).

**Handling of unsupported methods (501)**
The page doesn't mention 501 explicitly. It says the handler calls a method named from the request, e.g. "for the request method `SPAM`, the `do_SPAM()` method will be called", and that `BaseHTTPRequestHandler` "must be subclassed to handle each request method". The 501 response for a missing `do_*()` method is implemented in the source but not documented here. `SimpleHTTPRequestHandler` only implements `do_GET()` and `do_HEAD()`.

**server_address**
The page documents it only as the first constructor argument: `HTTPServer(server_address, RequestHandlerClass)`. In the example it is a tuple, `('', 8000)`. The `server_name` and `server_port` attributes are derived from it, and `server_port` is "obtained from *server_address*".

**close_connection**
> "Boolean that should be set before `handle_one_request()` returns, indicating if another request may be expected, or if the connection should be shut down."

**ThreadingHTTPServer daemon_threads**
`daemon_threads` is **not mentioned** on this page. The page says only that the class "is identical to HTTPServer but uses threads to handle requests by using the `ThreadingMixIn`. This is useful to handle web browsers pre-opening sockets, on which `HTTPServer` would wait indefinitely." It was added in 3.7. For the `daemon_threads` setting, check the `socketserver.ThreadingMixIn` documentation or the source.

**Example**
```python
def run(server_class=HTTPServer, handler_class=BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    server_address = ('', 8000)
    httpd = server_class(server_address, handler_class)
    httpd.serve_forever()
```

# sqlite3 docs (Python 3.15): thread-sharing and transaction control

## `check_same_thread`
From `sqlite3.connect()`:

> "If `True` (default), `ProgrammingError` will be raised if the database connection is used by a thread other than the one that created it. If `False`, the connection may be accessed in multiple threads; write operations may need to be serialized by the user to avoid data corruption. See `threadsafety` for more information."

## `threadsafety`
> "Integer constant required by the DB-API 2.0, stating the level of thread safety the `sqlite3` module supports. This attribute is set based on the default threading mode the underlying SQLite library is compiled with."

| SQLite mode | `threadsafety` | `SQLITE_THREADSAFE` | DB-API 2.0 meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| single-thread | 0 | 0 | Threads may not share the module |
| multi-thread | 1 | 2 | Threads may share the module, but not connections |
| serialized | 3 | 1 | Threads may share the module, connections and cursors |

The SQLite mode descriptions are:
- **Single-thread:** "SQLite is unsafe to use in more than a single thread at once."
- **Multi-thread:** "SQLite can be safely used by multiple threads provided that no single database connection is used simultaneously in two or more threads."
- **Serialized:** "SQLite can be safely used by multiple threads with no restriction."

*Changed in 3.11:* "Set threadsafety dynamically instead of hard-coding it to `1`."

**Thread-sharing guidance:** keep `check_same_thread=True` unless necessary. If you set it to `False`, check `sqlite3.threadsafety`. Only level 3 (serialized) allows sharing connections and cursors freely. Otherwise, serialize access yourself. `Connection.interrupt()` is the one method designed to be called from another thread, to abort running queries.

## `autocommit` (added in 3.12) vs `isolation_level`
`connect()` parameters:
- **autocommit:** "Control PEP 249 transaction handling behaviour... *autocommit* currently defaults to `LEGACY_TRANSACTION_CONTROL`. The default will change to `False` in a future Python release."
- **isolation_level:** "Control legacy transaction handling behaviour... Can be `"DEFERRED"` (default), `"EXCLUSIVE"` or `"IMMEDIATE"`; or `None` to disable opening transactions implicitly. Has no effect unless `Connection.autocommit` is set to `LEGACY_TRANSACTION_CONTROL` (the default)."

`Connection.autocommit` has three values:
- **`False`**: PEP 249-compliant, "`sqlite3` ensures a transaction is always open. Use `commit()` and `rollback()` to close transactions." This is "the recommended value."
- **`True`**: SQLite's autocommit mode. "`commit()` and `rollback()` have no effect in this mode."
- **`LEGACY_TRANSACTION_CONTROL`**: pre-3.12 behavior, governed by `isolation_level`. This is currently the default.

"Changing `autocommit` to `False` will open a new transaction, and changing it to `True` will commit any pending transaction."

`isolation_level` note: "Using `autocommit` to control transaction handling is recommended over using `isolation_level`." If not overridden in `connect()`, the default is `""`, an alias for `"DEFERRED"`.

## Implicit transaction behavior
`Cursor.execute()`:

> "If `autocommit` is `LEGACY_TRANSACTION_CONTROL`, `isolation_level` is not `None`, *sql* is an `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, or `REPLACE` statement, and there is no open transaction, a transaction is implicitly opened before executing *sql*."

`executemany()` uses the same implicit handling. `executescript()`: in legacy mode with a pending transaction, "an implicit `COMMIT` statement is executed first. No other implicit transaction control is performed."

Other related points:
- `commit()`/`rollback()`: do nothing if `autocommit` is `True` or no transaction is open. If `autocommit` is `False`, a new transaction is opened afterward.
- `close()`: with `autocommit=False`, a pending transaction is rolled back. With `True` or legacy mode, no implicit transaction control is executed, so commit first.
- **Context manager:** commits on success and rolls back on exception, but "neither implicitly opens a new transaction nor closes the connection." It does nothing if `autocommit` is `True`.

```python
con = sqlite3.connect("app.db", autocommit=False)  # PEP 249 behavior
with con:
    con.execute("INSERT INTO lang(name) VALUES(?)", ("Python",))
con.close()
```

**Note:** the page was truncated, so the full "Explanation → Transaction control" section is not included here beyond its opening recommendation to set `autocommit=False` via `connect()`.

**Caveat:** I read the docs through WebFetch, which summarises pages and skips some details. I checked the source behaviours (daemon_threads, send_error, the 501 path) against the local Python 3.9.6 stdlib. That version is older than the contract's 3.11+ floor, so re-check those on 3.11+. I did not search the bug tracker.

## Key findings

**1. Shutdown**
1. `BaseServer.shutdown()` blocks until `serve_forever()` stops. It must be called from a different thread than the one running `serve_forever()`, or it deadlocks. The docs example runs `serve_forever` in a thread and calls `shutdown()` from the main thread.
2. Python signal handlers always run in the main thread, and `signal.signal()` can only be called from the main thread (otherwise `ValueError`). If `serve_forever()` runs in the main thread, a handler that calls `shutdown()` deadlocks. This is the trap.
3. Two patterns work:
   - **A, recommended:** run `serve_forever()` in a worker thread. The main thread installs the handlers, then waits on a `threading.Event`. The handler only calls `event.set()`. After the wait, the main thread calls `server.shutdown()`, then `server.server_close()`, then `db.close()`, then `sys.exit(0)`.
   - **B:** keep `serve_forever()` in the main thread. The handler starts a short-lived thread that calls `shutdown()`.
   - Pattern A avoids calling any lock-taking code inside a handler. The signal docs warn that `threading.Lock` inside a handler can deadlock.
   - The main thread must wait with a timeout loop (for example `while not ev.wait(0.5)`) so signal handlers get a chance to run.
4. Per the source, `ThreadingHTTPServer` sets `daemon_threads=True` and `block_on_close=True` by default. The docs say `server_close()` waits for non-daemon threads (the `daemon_threads` default was checked in the 3.9.6 source). With daemon threads, `server_close()` returns even if keep-alive handler threads are blocked in `readline`.
5. Keep-alive connections do not block exit because the handler threads are daemons. The process exits when the main thread returns. Pending request threads are simply abandoned.
6. Windows signals:
   - `signal.signal()` accepts only SIGABRT, SIGFPE, SIGILL, SIGINT, SIGSEGV, SIGTERM and SIGBREAK. Other signals raise `ValueError`, and POSIX-only names such as SIGUSR1 are not defined (`AttributeError`).
   - `CTRL_BREAK_EVENT` and `CTRL_C_EVENT` are valid only as arguments to `os.kill()`. They are not handler targets. The receiving process sees `SIGBREAK` or `SIGINT`.
   - The docs say nothing about how SIGTERM is delivered on Windows.
   - `subprocess.CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP` was not fetched. From general knowledge, not confirmed here, a test harness needs `creationflags=CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP` to send `CTRL_BREAK_EVENT` to the child without hitting itself.
7. Register handlers defensively with `getattr(signal, "SIGBREAK", None)` and `getattr(signal, "SIGTERM", None)`. Register SIGINT everywhere.

**2. sqlite3**
1. `check_same_thread=True` is the default and raises `ProgrammingError` when another thread uses the connection. With `False`, the docs say writes "may need to be serialized by the user".
2. `sqlite3.threadsafety` reflects the SQLite build. A value of 3 means serialized mode, where connections can be shared freely. A value of 1 means connections must not be shared. This machine reports 1, so the spec must not rely on SQLite's own serialization.
3. Design options:
   - **Single connection** with `check_same_thread=False` and one `threading.Lock` around every execute/commit pair. This is simplest and safe, and it satisfies R14. SQLite serializes writes anyway.
   - **Per-thread connections** (threading.local) avoid the lock, but they need cleanup, and every connection pays the open and pragma cost on each new thread. Handler threads are one per connection.
4. Transaction control:
   - `autocommit=` exists only in 3.12+, so it cannot be relied on under a 3.11 floor.
   - The portable choice is `isolation_level=None`, which means SQLite autocommit. Each statement is its own atomic, durable transaction.
   - The single-statement click `UPDATE links SET clicks = clicks + 1, last_clicked_at = ? WHERE slug = ?` is then atomic. No explicit `commit()` is needed.
   - With the default legacy mode, an implicit transaction opens before UPDATE/INSERT/DELETE and stays open until `commit()`. Forgetting `commit()` loses data on restart.
5. Atomic increment: the single UPDATE statement is the atomic increment. The lock only needs to cover the connection. Check `cursor.rowcount` to detect a deleted slug.
6. A resolve is a SELECT (to check expiry) followed by an UPDATE. Under the lock, hold both together for correctness. Otherwise a link could expire or be deleted between the two steps.
7. Journal mode: the default (DELETE) journal is durable and fine for this use. WAL is optional. WAL adds `-wal` and `-shm` side files, which matter if a test inspects or copies the DB file after shutdown. Closing the last connection normally checkpoints and removes the WAL files.
8. Durability across restart: with autocommit mode, committed data survives. Always call `conn.close()` on shutdown. AC2 checks the DB for the SHA-256 digest, and it opens the file externally. Autocommit means the data is visible to the external reader immediately.
9. Set `PRAGMA user_version = 1` once at DB creation, plus `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`.
10. `PRAGMA foreign_keys` is off by default and the contract does not require it.

**3. http.server**
1. `protocol_version` defaults to `'HTTP/1.0'`. HTTP/1.1 permits persistent connections but then "must include an accurate Content-Length" on every response.
2. Under HTTP/1.0 every connection closes after one response, so the shutdown problem with open keep-alive connections does not arise. The contract does not mandate keep-alive. HTTP/1.1 plus `Content-Length: 0` on 204 and 302 is safer for clients that reuse connections.
3. `Content-Length: 0` on 204 and 302 must be set explicitly with `send_header`. `send_error` is not used for these.
4. `send_error()` (from the 3.9.6 source) always sends `Connection: close`. It also sends an HTML body, not the contract's JSON error shape.
   - Do not use `send_error` for contract errors.
   - Write a custom JSON responder that sets `Content-Type`, `Content-Length` and, for 413, `Connection: close`.
   - For 413 also set `self.close_connection = True`. Without that, a persistent HTTP/1.1 connection would try to parse the unread body as the next request.
5. For 413, check `Content-Length > 8192` before calling `rfile.read`, and never read the body. This matches the contract.
6. Read the body with `int(headers.get('Content-Length') or 0)` and `rfile.read(n)`. A non-numeric or negative `Content-Length` needs a defined behaviour. The contract is silent, so the spec should say (suggest 400 `invalid_request`).
7. `handle_one_request` returns 501 through `send_error` when `do_<METHOD>` is missing. The contract demands 404 `not_found` for any unlisted (method, path) pair. So define `do_HEAD`, `do_PUT`, `do_PATCH`, `do_OPTIONS` and `do_DELETE` and `do_POST` and `do_GET`, all routing to one dispatcher.
   - Alternatively override `handle_one_request`, or set `do_*` dynamically by iterating over a method list.
   - HEAD needs care: `send_error` omits the body for HEAD, but a custom responder should still send the 404 headers. Whether to write a body on HEAD is a spec decision.
   - Arbitrary unknown method tokens (for example `FOO`) still get 501. An `__getattr__` on the handler for names starting with `do_` can cover that.
8. Logging: override `log_message` to a no-op or to `sys.stderr`. Defaults already go to stderr, never stdout, so the stdout rule is satisfied even with defaults. Python 3.12+ scrubs control characters in the log text.
9. Binding: `ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)` then `server.server_address[1]` gives the real port. Bind failure raises `OSError`, which maps to exit 3. Catch it around construction.
10. The ready line must be printed after binding and flushed: `print(..., flush=True)`. Do not print anything else to stdout.
11. A bind or DB-open failure must print a message to stderr and exit 3. An argparse error exits 2 by default.
12. Set `allow_reuse_address` (the default on `HTTPServer` is 1). Setting `request_queue_size` higher than the default 5 may help the 50-concurrent-request test (AC11).

## Constraints the spec MUST respect
- Do not call `shutdown()` from the thread running `serve_forever()`. Handlers must only set an event, or hand off to another thread.
- Install signal handlers in the main thread. Register SIGBREAK only if `hasattr(signal, "SIGBREAK")`, and SIGTERM defensively.
- All sqlite access must go through one lock-protected connection or per-thread connections. Do not rely on `sqlite3.threadsafety`.
- The `autocommit=` keyword is not available on 3.11. Use `isolation_level=None`, or call `commit()` explicitly.
- Never use `send_error` for contract errors. It sends HTML and forces `Connection: close`.
- If `protocol_version` is HTTP/1.1, every response needs an accurate `Content-Length`, including `0` on 204 and 302.
- Define `do_*` methods for every method the contract treats as 404, otherwise `http.server` returns 501.
- Stdout is reserved for the ready line. Do not use `print` for diagnostics.

## Recommendations for the spec
1. Specify pattern A for shutdown: a worker thread runs `serve_forever`, the main thread waits on an Event, and the sequence is `shutdown()`, `server_close()`, `conn.close()`, `exit(0)`.
2. Specify `daemon_threads = True` explicitly on the server subclass, even though it is the default. Also set `block_on_close = False` to guarantee `server_close()` returns promptly with keep-alive sockets open.
3. Specify one `sqlite3.connect(db, check_same_thread=False, isolation_level=None)` plus one `threading.Lock`. The resolve path holds the lock across SELECT and UPDATE.
4. Specify `protocol_version = "HTTP/1.1"` with a mandatory `Content-Length` helper used by every response path. State what happens on a 413 (`Connection: close`, `close_connection = True`, body unread).
5. Specify a single `_dispatch()` called from every `do_*` method for GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD and OPTIONS. State HEAD behaviour: 404 headers with no body, or the same as GET with no body.
6. Specify handling of malformed `Content-Length` (missing means empty per the contract; non-integer or negative needs a rule).
7. Specify the bind-and-open order: open the DB (exit 3 on error), bind (exit 3 on `OSError`), print the ready line, install signal handlers and start serving. Installing handlers before the ready line is also fine. The ordering that matters is that handlers are installed before the ready line is printed. A test may send SIGINT immediately after reading it.
8. Specify the Windows test harness: spawn with `creationflags=subprocess.CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP` (not verified here) and send `os.kill(pid, signal.CTRL_BREAK_EVENT)`.
9. Specify `log_message` as a stderr write, or a no-op, with nothing on stdout.
